utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we return into closed session to hear the remainder of the the evidence of the the present witness, I'd like to briefly deal with a few procedural matters. Yesterday, Mr. Bakrac, there was the the issue of reconsidering your position about the source of some of the documents you tendered through Mr. Theunens. Any further report on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I went over the documents again, over the documents enumerated by you. There were nine of them. As for D183 and D195, we sent a request yesterday to the National Council to check and to tell us whether the previous Defence team had received those documents from them, whether they had been disclosed. And then there remain nine documents which I -- which I said were received from potential witnesses. I said that clumsily. I went over those documents yesterday and I established that in relation to four documents we can address the National Council because those are documents from the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of the Interior, and Palilula municipality. Therefore, National Council could be of assistance in that matter. There remain four documents from private sources and the persons that provided us those four documents were identified by me clumsily as potential witnesses. However, they are simply persons who gave us permission to use those documents, without either me or Mr. Petrovic talking to them at length to see whether there is a potential for calling them as witnesses for the Defence. So this involves the last four documents which are D167, D192, D191, and D182. These four, if you agree, could be admitted later on in the trial. And I propose this knowing full well that you can refuse to admit them based on the fact that we are not disclosing information about their provenance. As for the other documents, I request the National Council to provide us with a reply within maximum of 14 days to see whether these documents could be found in the archives of the institutions I enumerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, for the others you say we can address the relevant ministries, apparently you did not receive it from them. You also received it from private sources but on the basis of the content of those documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore you are just not willing to tell us from whom you got all these documents. So apart from whether there's an opportunity to verify whether the same document is found in any archives, but you're just saying, I'm not going to tell you from whom I got them. That's on the record. The Chamber will consider how to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely so. These four documents come from Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina. I'm not aware whether archives exist. We will try to verify that as well. Perhaps it sounds a bit arrogant that I do not wish to disclose the source of information, but I'm simply trying to be cautious. And should these witnesses indeed -- should these persons indeed become witness, we will try to admit the documents through them. On two of these documents it can be seen that the document was sent to the person named in the documents. D167 says so clearly. The name of the person is indicated there. But I wish to proceed cautiously until these people become indeed our witnesses, knowing full well that you could refuse to admit these documents into evidence later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the Chamber suggests to you that you would withdraw the tendering of all of these documents. And that once the conditions are fulfilled, that is, whether you have found similar copies in archives or that you do not even know whether these archives exist or whether you call anyone for those -- anyone to introduce them as witnesses, therefore if you withdraw, there is no prejudice in re-tendering them at a later stage and then we'll see whether we use the same numbers. But if you would not do that, you should not be surprised if the Chamber would deny admission of all of them. And I'm talking about the ones you received from the private sources. I'm not talking about the RFA related documents because we do understand that you are handicapped there by not knowing exactly what the history is. So we'll leave that for the time being. We might leave that open. But I'm talking about the other ones, the ones you just mentioned where you will address ministries in order to see whether the same or similar documents are found and the ones where you say, we would have to further consider with those who provided those documents whether or not we could use them. But my suggestion is that you withdraw the tendering of all these documents without prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you kindly tell me whether the Chamber prefer me to do that in writing or can I do it orally? Can I make this withdrawal orally until we receive what you said we should receive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, if you want to withdraw the tendering of those documents orally, you can do it. It's then on the record. And of course it will then be -- this withdrawal will be referred to in the decision with Theunens' documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these four documents coming from private sources for which I cannot establish quickly whether they exist in any archives, could I then withdraw their tendering. And the remaining four and 183 and 195, we should then wait for the National Council's response, because we had already requested their response, and we expect their response within seven days. So that's what pertains to those four documents. And the remaining four, which had been issued by different countries, different states, then I'm hereby applying to withdraw their tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, the others, I suggested that you withdraw the others as well, but of course you're not in any way bound to follow any suggestions. But the Chamber is not in a position to say whether you should or should not follow that suggestion. The four are on the record. We'll see what we'll do with the others. Then I move on. Housekeeping session, we are thinking on having a housekeeping session on the 23rd of February, but we would first inquire with the parties whether that creates any problem. Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've forgotten completely what date it is today. 9th, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be Wednesday in two weeks from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were hoping, to be honest, that we would have the housekeeping sooner rather than later. I had hoped to head to Belgrade to begin Defence preparations in the next two weeks. But if that isn't possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying -- that's exactly the reason why we're asking you. That's -- you would rather have it earlier than --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My plan was to leave in around 10 to 14 days. If it could be had within that period, that would be good for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I give you our position, could you first give us an indication as to when we would have 92 bis hearings -- 98 bis hearings, otherwise 23rd of February is fine with us, but we first need to know about the 98 bis hearings in order to give you our position. Looking at it from today's perspective, the 23rd is fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And earlier, as Mr. Jordash suggested, would that cause you any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the week starting the 21st of February is fine with us. The 23rd is a Wednesday, the 21st is a Monday, and this -- if this is what Mr. Jordash had in mind, that's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Jordash had on his mind the week before that. Mr. Jordash, could you please -- you were heading for the second half of next week, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I certainly will be around all of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see an obstacle, I don't see a conflict. I would like to know so that my colleague and I can plan the 98 bis submissions, but I don't see a problem for holding it a week earlier, perhaps at the end of the week preceding that, say Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see. Mr. Groome, any preference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be ready at any date set by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider it and we'll inform the parties already about the housekeeping session this week, but a Scheduling Order for the following procedural steps may be issued only next week. Of course, the one is also related to the other because we cannot think about 98 bis until the case of the Prosecution has been closed. I have no further matters at this moment. I have still got two times ten minutes for you, Mr. Jordash, but I'd rather keep that, for the time being, most likely later today. Because if I understood you well, Mr. Groome, for the next witness half an hour was the new schedule for examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think the more accurate estimate at this stage would be about 40 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40 minutes. Do I also understand that the Stanisic Defence does not intend to cross-examination the next witness, if matters do not change?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If matters do not change, then no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the same is true for the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not cross-examine either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will -- Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I also indicate that we will only seek to advance submissions on the one point which is the issue relating to the addition of exhibits to the 65 ter and admission into the courtroom of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 20th motion, and you are not going to make any submissions about the other matter which we would have to hear anyhow in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The other matter, it occurred to us that we were not going to be seeking a remedy or any direction or order from the Court which would assist the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. So one times ten minutes are off. We turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jordash, ten minutes' oral submission on the Prosecution's 20th motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list and for admission of exhibits from the bar table with confidential annexes filed 21st of January, 2011. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The application is opposed. We oppose the application but also are mindful of previous rulings which mean that the merits of the application appear to fall fairly and squarely with the Prosecution, but nonetheless, we oppose the application. We oppose the application on two principled basis. Firstly, that the Prosecution have not demonstrated that the application is in the interests of justice, and in particular that the accused's right to be informed of the charges is effectively trampled, we would submit, by the application, or by the grant of the application. And, secondly, that - and this is a subset, as such, of the first - that the prejudice to the accused cannot at this stage be remedied. And, thirdly -- I know I said two, but thirdly, that the Prosecution have failed to show good cause for the application being made at this stage. Dealing with the first, the interests of justice generally. The application, we submit, must, as we've submitted before, be seen in light of the -- what we would characterise as massive disclosures which have occurred during this case. In particular, we submit that the Prosecution have effectively continuously been allowed to disclose and rely upon new evidence, which, even putting aside the Mladic diaries, runs into the hundreds of pages, but with the Mladic diaries runs into thousands of pages. The Prosecution's application effectively seeks to reduce the accused's right to be informed of the charges to a right to be informed of the charges at some time during the Prosecution case. It is the Prosecution's submission that providing -- and it has been the Prosecution's submission throughout, that providing the Defence has an opportunity to investigate the late disclosed material, then no prejudice arises. In our submission, that's completely incorrect. Of course there is the prejudice which arises through late disclosure, causing significant investigation and work by the Defence team to meet that evidence. The thousands of pages which I referred to a moment ago has given rise and will continue to give rise to hundreds of hours of new work for a Defence team which has finite resources. The case commenced on a certain basis with a certain volume of material. The resources allocated were based on that volume. And at some point, when the disclosures reach a certain size, those resources must clearly become inadequate. But in our submission that is only one of the prejudices which arise through the late disclosure of a volume of material, and especially material that's served at the close of the Prosecution case. And those clearly concern what the right to be informed of the charges is principally about, which is that an accused has a right to be informed of the detail of the charges promptly, and that is before the commencement of the Prosecution case. Whilst of course there will be exceptions, what ought to be an exception, in our submission, has now become the norm. The Prosecution motion, in our submission, selects only an aspect of the prejudice, because the remainder of the prejudice, in our submission, cannot, as the Prosecution case is about to end, be rectified. And that's particularly pertinent in the case of the Pecanac collection. The Prosecution accept that they cannot establish even authenticity with those documents. So at the close of the Prosecution case, the Prosecution want to introduce documents which they accept they cannot establish authenticity and that is another consequence of the fact of the late application prejudice to the process as well as prejudice to the Defence. In terms of -- if I just may quickly deal with the material. The Prosecution's application suggests, in relation to the narrow prejudice which they seek to deal with in paragraph 8, that the work that arises from these documents will be insignificant. That's clearly not the case. In relation to the Banja Luka collection, Document 2 introduces a meeting, not before relied upon, between Mladic, Kovac, and the alleged co-ordinator of the MUP Serbian forces Dragan Filipovic. Documents 3, 4, 5, and 6 concern a whole new operation which I haven't or cannot recall hearing of before, Operation Kosovski Bozuri. Document 7 deals with new activities in relation to Mrkonjic Grad. Of the Pecanac collection, similar problems or similar difficulties will arise but exacerbated by the lack of authenticity or authenticating indices on any of the documents. Documents which are, on the face of them, highly incriminatory and on the other hand conceded by the Prosecution as having insufficient authenticating indices. Nonetheless requiring investigation by the Defence on an individual basis, requiring interviewing of witnesses, requiring taking instructions from the client. These few pages, as characterised by the Prosecution, giving rise to tens and tens of legal hours to ensure that the allegations contained therein are met. Finally, the lack of good cause. The Prosecution, in our submission, have not even got off the ground when it comes to demonstrating good cause. If one reads the application, or the motion, the Prosecution, in our submission, don't even attempt to demonstrate good cause, simply indicating dates when they received the material, intervening periods of many months, before the material is then sought to be relied upon in the courtroom. In our submission -- in our submission, that says one of two things: Either a lack of due diligence by the Prosecution and therefore no good cause or diligence by the Prosecution which demonstrates eloquently, in our submission, how much work the Prosecution did and had to do to assess this evidence and how much corresponding work the Defence will have to do to meet it. One or the other must be the case. Those are our submissions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Could I first inquire as to whether the witness has arrived. First we take a break. If he was on his way, then he certainly -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break first. Now, in view of what we could expect after the break, do the parties - I'm also looking at Mr. Stanisic - do they intend to have the full break of half an hour? Or would we -- expecting that we would not be in court for any more than 40 minutes, 45 minutes, or would we do, well, let's say 20 or 25 minutes' break, which would give an early release for all of us?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could the break be limited to 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking around. Also change of tapes, et cetera. 20 minutes, 22 minutes, if we would then reconvene at 20 minutes past 5.00. I'm looking at Madam Registrar, whether that causes any problems. No. We'll have a break and we resume at 20 minutes past 5.00. --- Break taken at 4.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked the parties to briefly confer with me because we have one functionality not functioning, that's the e-court transcript system is not available to the parties. However, we do have a transcript being made; we can see that on the other screen. There is a possibility to have access to exhibits. And under those circumstances, rather than to wait for another 10, 15, 20 minutes until the system would be fully functional again, with the consent of the parties the Chamber decided to proceed. Who is it who will examine the next witness? Ms. Friedman, will it be you?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. And from your schedule I take it that it is Saidin Salkic that the Prosecution's calling.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Salkic. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually understand you speaking English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would prefer to give your testimony in English, I don't know whether that is what you want to choose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be more appropriate in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well I leave the choice entirely to you. If you feel at any moment uncomfortable with using the English language, although I see that it would not cause any serious problems, then please tell us. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by the usher. And I would now like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that you expected to have the English text. And of course I do --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please be seated, Mr. Salkic. But the words are the same in the two languages. Do you -- are you tuned in on the English channel or on the B/C/S channel and is that the channel you would prefer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm still getting the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we -- could the witness be put on Channel 4. That's the English channel, Mr. Salkic. Comfortable now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you can call it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that it's not really comfortable being in that position and about to start your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we understand that. Ms. Friedman, are you ready to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, you'll first be examined by Ms. Friedman. Ms. Friedman is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: My name is Saidin Salkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, do you recall giving a statement to an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 22nd and 28th of July, 2005?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: I do not recall the date exactly, but, yes, I do remember. It was 2005, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity prior to testifying today to review this statement in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Is there anything you wish to change in that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you give the same answers in substance as what is contained in that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: I think so. There would be maybe more pain or something as the time has gone by. But factually, I wouldn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 6120, the statement of Saidin Salkic dated 22nd and 28th July, 2005, bearing ERN 0423-8898, 0423-8909, into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P2488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2488 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the Prosecution also tenders a 92 ter associated exhibit, 65 ter 1228.5, which contains two video stills taken from the Skorpion's video admitted as P2161. The witness indicates in his statement that he was shown 21 video stills bearing ERN 0363-9681, 0363-9721, and that he recognised his father Sidik Salkic in six of them. Four of these stills were already admitted through 92 bis witnesses. So in order to avoid duplication, we are seeking the admission of the remaining two only. The four that have been admitted are photos 9, 10, and 16 in P1796, and photo 19 in P1870. The remaining two stills are -- that we now tender are photo 15, ERN 0363-9709, and that's at time code 14757 of the Skorpions video, and photo 21, ERN 0363-9721, which is at time code 15414 of the Skorpions video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the two stills can receive one number? They can be united in one exhibit, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to the two remaining photographs, numbers 15 and 21, would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2489 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Salkic, we have to go through these more or less administrative matters. We have to do that very carefully. Ms. Friedman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's instructions of the 18th of February, 2010, at this time I will present a public summary of the evidence contained in Mr. Salkic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that you've explained to Mr. Salkic that that's not his evidence but this is just to inform the public about what your evidence is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Saidin Salkic is from Srebrenica town. As a child, he lived there with his father, mother, and sister. In the beginning of July 1995, his family was still living at home under difficult circumstances and hardly had anything to eat. On the 11th of July, as word spread that Muslims from Srebrenica were being taken away, many found refuge in the Salkic family's home. Everyone was worried and panicked and spoke about how they had to leave because the Serbs were taking over Srebrenica. The men went in the direction of Jaglici, while the women, children, and elderly went to Potocari. That is the last day Saidin Salkic saw his father. His father gave him a pocket watch before setting out with the witness's uncle and other men. The witness went with his mother, sister, and grandmother to Potocari, where they spent a couple of days eating honey to survive. While in Potocari, Serb soldiers separated out young boys from the group, and the witness could hear young girls screaming. On the 13th of July, many buses arrived to take the refugees away. There were barricades up, with UN soldiers and Serb soldiers standing next to and behind the barricades. Saidin Salkic and his family boarded one of the buses and were taken in an unknown direction. At a certain point, the buses were stopped and boarded by Serb soldiers wearing green uniforms who told them to get out and ordered them to walk to Kladanj. Only years later, in June 2005, the witness saw video footage of Srebrenica on the news and recognised his father.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, have I summarised your statement accurately?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: If that's possible, yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I will now ask you some additional questions. First, how old were you at the time of these incidents?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Thirteen I guess.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 13. I was born in 1981, so you do the counting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 5, you state that your father left home with your uncle, Beriz Salkic.

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your uncle?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen him alive since that time?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: No. Only in my dreams.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were other male family members with you and your family in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Who was with you?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: It was my grandmother, my cousins.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did all of your family members leave Potocari?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: No. My uncle never came. He was in Potocari. And some of my childhood friends, I never saw again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm having a -- I'm a little confused about to whom I'm speaking to. And that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I speak away from the microphone. But, yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please come as close to the microphone - and could the microphones be adjusted - because your words have to be translated for those who do not understand English. And the only way of hearing your voice is through the microphones, so therefore the interpreters are asking for speaking up. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 7, you stated that while you were in Potocari your grandmother wanted to disguise you as a girl so that you wouldn't be taken away but you were too ashamed to do so. My question for you is whether at any point someone did try to take you away?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, actually. As we were walking towards the buses, I heard the sound of a voice saying, You, kid on the side, and I just moved on the side, and then my mother saw that and she walked back and she started screaming, crying, and doing everything. And then a lot of men gathered around and had their guns out and pointed at my mother, me, until a voice said -- the man said, He's too young, he can go, and I proceeded to go to the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has admitted into evidence in this case P2161, the Skorpions video, which includes footage of members the Skorpions unit executing six Bosnian Muslim men and boys. Mr. Salkic, is this the video footage that you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When did you first find out that it existed?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it says in the statement, I just saw the news briefing on television and I saw men coming off the truck and I sensed my father. I couldn't be sure first, in those few seconds, but I sensed it was him. And I ran home to tell mom about it. And then a few days later -- we kind of lived in hope that it wasn't him, but a few days later it was confirmed. More video was shown. Yeah, it was my father.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You've said also in your statement that he was the one wearing the blue shirt. Did you recognise this shirt?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, yes, and I -- I -- every time now I see somebody in a blue shirt, I think of him. Yeah, I did recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, would the Court Usher please display 65 ter 6159. Your Honours, this is a demonstrative exhibit, ERN 0679-6454, which contains information about the victims of the Trnovo killing. It's the subject of an agreed fact filed -- between the parties, filed on 15 February 2010 and contained in Annex A, part N. This exhibit contains video stills of each of the victims taken, again, from P2161, along with brief biographical information, including their dates of birth and the locations where they were living in 1991 according to the census. I've spoken with the Defence and they do not object to it. So we tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number of this exhibit would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be P2490, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I took the silence from the Defence as being an agreement with what just was told to the Court by Ms. Friedman. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I will now ask the witness to show the Chamber the locations mentioned on this exhibit and other location -- on the exhibit just admitted, and other locations that are important to his evidence. Would the Court Usher please display 65 ter 61610. This is page 35 of the Court binder containing maps related to the indictment. It is a map of the Srebrenica Bajina Basta area that has been marked -- annotated by Mr. Salkic. And this new version bears ERN 0679-6473. Can we zoom in, please, to the middle third, perhaps, of the map. Yes. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, prior to your testimony, were you asked to indicate the approximate location of several villages on the map that you see before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Near the words "Srebrenica" there is a letter F. What does the letter F represent?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: That is the place where I was living with my family. It's the first letter of the name Fojhar, which is a place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And there is an arrow leading away from Fojhar in a north-west direction, more west. What does this indicate?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: This indicates the direction where my father went from home.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the location Potocari is circled. Is that the location where you went with your mother and sister and others in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the Chamber can see where Azmir Alispahic and Juso Delic are from, because Srebrenica and Osmace, south-east of Srebrenica, are clearly marked on the map. But the remaining three victims are from towns which are not on the map, so I would like to ask you to assist with that.

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: I could. I could try.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Dino Salihovic is from Likari, Srebrenica. Can you explain where that is? Or we can also offer you a pen so you could circle the general vicinity.

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I was 13 and I never went to these villages. I was -- so I couldn't exactly point where it is. But I assume it is very close to Srebrenica. It's a -- it's kind of this perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And how long would it take to get from Likari to Srebrenica, approximately, by car or foot, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: People walked. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And Safet Fejzic is from Blazijevici, Srebrenica. Do you know where Blazijevici is?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't. But I think it's somewhere close to river Drina, I would assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, Smail Ibrahimovic from her Hrnici, Bratunac. Have you heard of that location?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And as you said, I think it's close to Bratunac, or closer than to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I tender this marked version of 65 ter 6160 as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P2491, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2491 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, have you spoken to the families of the other Trnovo victims?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: I -- yes, I have briefly once in Belgrade. But I feel them, and they -- we have this communication beyond words, I guess. Something that connects us and forever will.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, I only have one or two more questions for you. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the impact that the murder of your father has had on you and your family?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Well, my life changed. I got to understand it more, I got to appreciate it more, and realise how grand it is and how precious it is. The impact it had on my family and me is immeasurable. It's something you cannot speak. But you can feel things every day, every night. Hundreds of dreams with blood and with weirdness and undefinable things. It had impact on my mother, who stayed lonely since then. Who never met another man, who spends her days in solitude because that's how she is. She loved him. My sister went through her own personal hell. She was born in 1987. She was younger than me. She was a girl. And I can only through my hell of it understand hers. And I'm sure it was as mad as it was for me. And some things are just how they are, you know. I sometimes drive on sunny days - I mentioned this before - and drive to buy a packet of milk and sometimes it seems like nothing has happened. You get the feeling of beauty of the life, the rhythm, and it's all beautiful, and there's just this ever-present weirdness about these people who have been wiped out of part of our lives. And they'll never change, they'll always stay like that. And however you try to be happy, and you naturally do because it's in the man to try, there's that thing that will always be with us. And I thought that over time it would heal, and it does, time does heal certain things, but then other things are clearer, you know. What my father went through, I could experience it clearly, so intensely and so often. And that's always there. Every time I drink water I think of him, because the last thing he said, he said, Give us some water and then kill us. And every time I drink water I think of him. As I said, every time I see somebody in a blue shirt I think of him. And I always will. I'm getting used to living with that. I have no choice. It's -- in a way, it makes me stronger. It makes me want to drink water with more passion. It makes me want to do things with more passion. It makes me appreciate the truth and how grand it is. I mean, everything is enhanced. Nothing is the same. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And do you know whether these murders have had similar impacts on the other families?

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: I can only imagine. I see them, you know, I see these women, these powerless, beautiful women who've made -- had their children, you know, and some had five disappear. I can only bow to them. I don't know. I think even them seeing me is a pain to them. I am aware of everything and it's not easy. Are we getting closer to the -- do you have more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: SAIDIN SALKIC
utterances.text: Because I have something to say too. From -- well, I'm a poet and I thought it was very important for me to say that for many of these people it is too late for justice that you can give them. I thought -- I was a kid, I couldn't have done anything, but I thought there was a will, there was a way to stop it, and there would have been justice, to stop the slaughter and genocide. And I think it's in the conscience of those who could have done that and didn't. And that will always stay on their conscience. I have my fight to fight and I do that the best way I can, try to love everybody. Wherever I went I found love. Every person in the world I've met, I found love in them. And for me this can be nothing but eternal crying, and it is. I don't know what else to do about it and what to think of it, how to understand it further. And I don't think there's justice for that. It will always be like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salkic, for giving your evidence. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Friedman. Is the situation, as far as the Defence, the same as announced before?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, we have no witnesses [sic]. But if I might express my client's sympathy for your loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Simatovic Defence case has no questions either. The least we can do and say in front of this witness, to express on behalf of ourselves and our clients our deepest regret for what has happened. And we deeply believe that the real culprit will be brought to justice and punished accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, usually if you are called by the Prosecution to testify, you will be cross-examined by the Defence if there's any reason to challenge your -- the testimony you've given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence teams have informed the Chamber and have repeated it a second ago that they have no questions for you, therefore are not challenging your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Chamber also has no questions for you, this concludes your evidence in this court. The Chamber fully understands that the experiences you've told us about and as we found them in your statement are of a kind that it will have been not easy for you, it will have been very painful, to again give us your testimony and to tell us what you experienced. I would like to thank you very much for engaging in this painful experience for you. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for having answered the questions that were put to you. And I wish you a safe journey back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you are invited to follow the usher, who will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since Mr. Salkic was the last witness called by the Prosecution, we came at a point that there's no further evidence presented, which does not mean that the Prosecution's case is already finally closed, because there are still quite a number of procedural issues outstanding. Some will be dealt with in writing, where some others will orally be dealt with. We'll inform the parties shortest notice about the date of the housekeeping session. And the parties can also expect, as I said before, a Scheduling Order to be issued most likely early next week. Is there any other procedural matter any of the parties would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day. I cannot tell you yet when we will resume, therefore the adjournment is sine die. The parties will be informed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.57 p.m.
